title: appendTable decides layout-vs-data once for a whole table, so one odd row flattens hundreds
acceptance: The layout-vs-data decision is made per row (rowCells.contains(where: cellHoldsBlockContent)) rather than once for the whole table
wikipedia_flag_gallery gains a .json expectation asserting the row structure survives and materially more than 225 of its 589 images are rescued, with landmark passages at start, middle and end

mdn_img_element and wikipedia_epub are re-frozen ONLY where the new output is genuinely better; the diff for each is inspected block by block and the reasoning recorded in PROVENANCE.md or the fixtures README
swift test green with all other fixtures passing unmodified
notes:
Filed from T-0055, which found this with a real capture and documented it under 'Known but unfixed: the flag table' in the fixtures README. Read that section first — it has the measurements.

The defect: `appendTable` evaluates `cells.contains(where: cellHoldsBlockContent)` once for the entire table, so a single atypical cell anywhere — a nested table for a multi-flag entry, say — flips every ordinary row into per-cell paragraph flattening. On the flag-list capture that yields 1,126 single-cell paragraph blocks and rescues only 225 of 589 images.

The product call, already made, so do not re-litigate it: judging per row is the more correct rule. Rows within one table genuinely can differ in kind, and a rule that lets the weirdest row dictate the treatment of hundreds of ordinary ones is wrong on its face. T-0055 left it alone only because its lease could not cover re-freezing two existing fixtures.

What is NOT settled, and is the real work here: `mdn_img_element` and `wikipedia_epub` were frozen against the old all-or-nothing behaviour and their output changes. Do not re-record them blindly — that would turn a regression guard into a rubber stamp. Read the before/after for each affected block, decide whether the new shape is actually better for a reader, and write down why. If either one gets worse, that is a finding worth reporting rather than absorbing.
